```{r}
#| label: setup

# Paths are from the repo root because _quarto.yml sets execute-dir: project.
library(tidyverse); library(arrow); library(broom)

source("r/f1_pole_model.R")   # the analysis: f1, races, rhos, m_grid, m_team
source("r/f1_pole_plot.R")    # the hero chart: by_grid, rho, drop_pct, hero

# Counts before the mart's filters, from the raw file.
# Check figures (vault, 17 Nov): 1,838 results, 15 pit-lane starts, 216 not classified.
raw        <- read_parquet("data/raw/f1/race_results.parquet")
classified <- !is.na(suppressWarnings(as.integer(raw$positionText)))  # a number = classified
n_all      <- nrow(raw)
n_pit      <- sum(as.integer(raw$grid) == 0)
n_dropped  <- sum(!classified)

# Short names for the numbers quoted in the text
fmt     <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(unname(x), format = "f", digits = digits)
num     <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
rho_ci  <- quantile(rhos, c(0.025, 0.975))
b_only  <- tidy(m_grid, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term == "grid")
b_car   <- tidy(m_team, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term == "grid")
r2_only <- glance(m_grid)$r.squared
r2_car  <- glance(m_team)$r.squared
pole    <- by_grid |> filter(grid == 1)

pole_finishes <- f1$finish_position[f1$grid == 1]   # finishing position of everyone who started on pole
n_pole        <- length(pole_finishes)               # how many pole-sitters finished the race
pole_win_pct  <- mean(pole_finishes == 1) * 100      # share who won
pole_top2_pct <- mean(pole_finishes <= 2) * 100      # share who finished 1st or 2nd

alt_text <- sprintf(
  "Dot chart of starting grid position (1 to 20) against median finishing position, with bars showing the middle half of finishes. The dots follow a dashed 'finish where you start' diagonal closely: the further back drivers start, the further back they finish (rank correlation %s). The bars are wide, so grid slot alone leaves plenty of room for surprises.",
  fmt(rho))
```

## Double Take: guess first

Before you scroll: a driver starts on pole. Where do they usually finish?

And if you scored how closely the finishing order follows the starting order, from 0 (no link at all) to 1 (identical every time), what score would you give it?

Write your guess down, then open the box.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Take a second look"}
Of the `r n_pole` drivers who started on pole and finished the race, **`r fmt(pole_win_pct, 0)`% won**, and `r fmt(pole_top2_pct, 0)`% finished first or second.

And how closely does the finishing order follow the starting order overall? 
On a scale from 0 (no link) to 1 (everyone finishes exactly where they started), it scores **`r fmt(rho)`**: a strong link, but far from a certainty. I guessed 0.37.
:::

```{r}
hero
```

**Take a second look:** Look at the right-hand side of the chart: drivers who start 15th or further back usually finish a few places *higher* than they started. Part of that gain is free: when cars ahead retire, everyone behind them moves up a place.

Some of it is also fast cars that started out of place, after a grid penalty or a bad qualifying, working their way back to where they belong.

## In plain English

Drivers who start near the front usually finish near the front. But fast cars qualify well *and* race well, so a lot of what looks like the power of pole position is really the power of the car.

## The technique

**Spearman's rank correlation** (family: association), then **linear regression with a covariate** (family: modelling).

Grid and finishing positions are both *ordinal*: the order matters, but the gap between 1st and 2nd isn't necessarily the same as between 15th and 16th. Spearman works on ranks, so it doesn't assume equal gaps. The regression then asks how much finishing position changes per grid place, first on its own and then comparing drivers in the same car (each team in each season counts as one car).

**Assumptions and checks**

| Assumption | How I checked | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Results are independent | Drivers in the same race are linked (only one can finish 1st) | The interval for the correlation resamples whole races. The regression's intervals will be too narrow, so treat them as rough |
| The relationship is roughly a straight line | Residuals-vs-fitted plot | The average miss stays near zero across the range: a straight line is a fair summary |
| Positions run from 1 to 20 | By design | Front-runners can finish far worse than predicted but not much better; noted as a limitation |
| Only classified finishers are included | `r n_pit` pit-lane starts and `r num(n_dropped)` non-classified results were dropped | Survivorship risk: see the caveats |

## What the numbers say

- Across `r num(nrow(f1))` classified finishes in `r nrow(races)` races (2022–2025), the rank correlation between grid and finish is **`r fmt(rho)`** (95% interval `r fmt(rho_ci[1])` to `r fmt(rho_ci[2])`, resampling whole races). That's a strong link.
- Ignoring the car, each place further back on the grid goes with finishing about **`r fmt(b_only$estimate)` places** further back (95% CI `r fmt(b_only$conf.low)` to `r fmt(b_only$conf.high)`). Grid alone explains `r fmt(r2_only * 100, 0)`% of the variation in finishing position.
- Comparing drivers in the same car, that falls to about **`r fmt(b_car$estimate)` places** (95% CI `r fmt(b_car$conf.low)` to `r fmt(b_car$conf.high)`): **`r fmt(drop_pct, 0)`% smaller**. Knowing the car raises the share explained to `r fmt(r2_car * 100, 0)`%.

## The brain trap: narrative fallacy

We like tidy stories: "he won because he started on pole". The start is visible and memorable; the car's pace across the whole weekend isn't, so the story gives the credit to the grid slot.

I fell for a version of it before running any code. I guessed the link was weak (0.37) and that the car explained little of it (8%). Both guesses were wrong in the same direction: I under-weighted the car.

## Verdict: Confounded

Grid and finish are strongly linked, but car pace drives both: fast cars qualify near the front *and* race near the front. Compare drivers in the same car and grid's effect shrinks by about `r fmt(drop_pct, 0)`%.

What's left still isn't proof that the grid slot itself causes better finishes. A driver who out-qualifies their team-mate may simply be quicker that weekend, and this model can't tell the two apart.

**What would change the verdict?** A case where grid slots move for reasons unrelated to speed, such as grid penalties for engine changes. Comparing penalised drivers with their own unpenalised races would isolate the grid slot itself.

## Echo

Same shape, different world: entrance-exam rank and final degree class (exhibit coming soon). Strong students enter near the top *and* graduate near the top, so the starting rank looks more powerful than it really is.

## Sources and caveats

- **Data:** [Jolpica F1 API](https://github.com/jolpica/jolpica-f1), race results 2022–2025, pulled 14–15 Nov 2026. Licence CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; the derived tables and this chart are shared under the same licence. n = `r num(nrow(f1))` classified finishes from `r num(n_all)` results. Unofficial data; F1 names are trademarks of Formula One Licensing B.V., and this site isn't affiliated with Formula 1.
- **Limitations:**
  - `r num(n_dropped)` results (`r fmt(n_dropped / n_all * 100, 1)`%) were dropped because the driver wasn't classified. If front-runners retire at a different rate from back-markers, that tilts the result (survivorship bias). Some late retirements still count as classified.
  - The regression's intervals are too narrow, because results within a race aren't independent.
  - "Same car" means the same team in the same season; it can't capture upgrades during a season or the difference between team-mates.
  - Positions are bounded at 1 and 20.
- **Synthetic?** No.
